title: Tables
text: This script builds the descriptive tables and exports every table in the analysis to tables/ as HTML. The exported tables are shown on the Results page.

title: Tables
text:
Table 1
Cases and controls are compared on the categorical variables (sex, transplanted organ, race, immunosuppression, CNS disease) and the continuous ones (age and the antibody levels, raw and log). tbl_summary() reports medians with interquartile ranges and counts with percentages. add_p() uses its defaults: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables, and Fisher’s exact or the χ² test for categorical ones, as described in the paper (Yoon et al. 2022). A second version is restricted to participants with antibody measurements.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create a Table 1 which compares cases in controls with regards to categorical and continuous variables
table1_all <- CleanData %>% select(CategoricalVariables, ContinuousVariables) %>%
  tbl_summary(by=CaseOrControl) %>%
  add_p() %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  bold_p()

#Create a Table 1 which compares cases in controls with regards to categorical and continuous variables, excluding pts with missing titers
table1_no_missing_titers <- CleanData_NoMissingTiters %>% select(CategoricalVariables, ContinuousVariables) %>%
  tbl_summary(by=CaseOrControl) %>%
  add_p() %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  bold_p()

section: AUC confidence intervals and optimal cutpoints

AUC confidence intervals and optimal cutpoints
The original analysis printed these results one at a time. Here they are collected into two summary tables using the helpers in Functions. The values are read directly from the objects created in Regression, ROC and cutpoints, not recomputed.

# Collect the AUC confidence intervals and optimal cutpoints computed in modeling.R
auc_ci_summary <- bind_rows(
  summarise_auc_ci(auc_ci_logtiter1_delong, auc_ci_logtiter1_bootstrap,
                   "Sex + log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM"),
  summarise_auc_ci(auc_ci_logtiter2_delong, auc_ci_logtiter2_bootstrap,
                   "log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM")
)

  summarise_cutpoint(cutpoint_gxm_igm, "GXM-IgM"),
  summarise_cutpoint(cutpoint_log_gxm_igm, "log GXM-IgM"),
  summarise_cutpoint(cutpoint_lam_igm, "Lam-IgM"),
  summarise_cutpoint(cutpoint_log_lam_igm, "log Lam-IgM")

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
text:
This script fits the logistic regression models relating cryptococcosis status to antibody levels, draws ROC curves for the multivariable models, and finds optimal titer cutpoints for GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM. Its tables and fitted objects are exported by Tables and Figures.
The outcome throughout is HasCryptococcus (case versus control). Odds ratios are exponentiated logistic regression coefficients. All analyses were exploratory, with no correction for multiple comparisons (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Univariable models on the original scale
text:
Univariable models on the original scale
tbl_uvregression() fits one logistic regression per candidate predictor: sex, race, corticosteroid, mycophenolate and mTOR inhibitor use, age, and the seven antibody levels on their original scale. Transplanted organ, calcineurin inhibitor use and CNS disease are left out. For context, CNS disease is recorded only for cases, and 43 of 44 participants received a calcineurin inhibitor (Yoon et al. 2022). An inline forest plot is added to each row.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Univariate regression tables utilizing titer
univariatetitertable<-CleanData %>%
  select(HasCryptococcus, CategoricalVariables, ContinuousVariables) %>%
  select(-CaseOrControl, -TransplantOrgan, -LogTiterVariables, -DrugCNI, -CNSDisease) %>%
  tbl_uvregression(method = glm, y = HasCryptococcus, method.args = list(family = binomial),
                   exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Multivariable model on the original scale
text:
Multivariable model on the original scale
A model with sex and Lam-IgM, merged side by side with the univariable table.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Multivariate model

mvtitermodel1 <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+LAMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData)

multivariatetitertable<-tbl_regression(mvtitermodel1, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()


#Prints the final regression table
regression_table_titer <- tbl_merge( tbls = list(univariatetitertable, multivariatetitertable), tab_spanner = c("**Univariate Model**", "**Multivariate Model**"))

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: ROC curve on the original scale
text:
ROC curve on the original scale
The model’s predicted probabilities are used to draw an ROC curve and compute its area under the curve (AUC). Predictions are made on the same data used to fit the model.


Click to show/hide R Code
#ROC curve
test_prob_titer = predict(mvtitermodel1, newdata = CleanData, type = "response")
titer_roc = pROC::roc(CleanData$HasCryptococcus ~ test_prob_titer, plot = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE)

section: Univariable models on the log scale
text:
Univariable models on the log scale
The same univariable analysis, with the log-transformed antibody levels in place of the original ones.


Click to show/hide R Code

univariatelogtitertable<-CleanData %>%
  select(HasCryptococcus, CategoricalVariables, ContinuousVariables) %>%
  select(-CaseOrControl, -TransplantOrgan, -TiterVariables, -DrugCNI, -CNSDisease) %>%

  add_inline_forest_plot()

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Multivariable models on the log scale
text:
Multivariable models on the log scale
Four models are fitted:



Model
Predictors




1
Sex + log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM


2
log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM (without sex)


3
Sex + log Lam-IgM


4

Model 1 is the paper’s main multivariable model. Model 2 checks that the higher proportion of women among cases is not driving the discrimination (Yoon et al. 2022). The univariable table is merged with models 1 and 2.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Multivariate modeling

mvlogtitermodel1 <-glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_LAMIgM+log_GXMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData)
mvlogtitermodel2<-glm(HasCryptococcus ~ log_LAMIgM+log_GXMIgM,
                      family = binomial, data=CleanData)
mvlogtitermodel3<-glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_LAMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData)
mvlogtitermodel4<-glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_GXMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData)


multivariatelogtitertable1<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel1, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

multivariatelogtitertable2<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel2, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

multivariatelogtitertable3<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel3, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

multivariatelogtitertable4<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel4, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()


#Prints the final logistic regression tables
regression_table_logtiter_1 <- tbl_merge( tbls = list(univariatelogtitertable, multivariatelogtitertable1), tab_spanner = c("**Univariate Model**", "**Multivariate Model**"))

regression_table_logtiter_2 <- tbl_merge( tbls = list(univariatelogtitertable, multivariatelogtitertable1, multivariatelogtitertable2 ), tab_spanner = c("**Univariate Model**", "**Multivariate Model 1**","**Multivariate Model 2**"))

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals
text:
ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals
ROC curves for models 1 and 2, as reported in the paper. Each AUC gets two 95% confidence intervals: DeLong’s analytic method and a bootstrap. The bootstrap resamples at random, so its limits can differ slightly between runs.


Click to show/hide R Code
#ROC curve 1
test_prob_logtiter1 = predict(mvlogtitermodel1, newdata = CleanData, type = "response")
logtiter_roc1 = pROC::roc(CleanData$HasCryptococcus ~ test_prob_logtiter1, plot = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE)

#Calculate 95% confidence intervals, both analytically and using bootstrapping
auc_ci_logtiter1_delong <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc1, method="delong")
auc_ci_logtiter1_bootstrap <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc1, method="bootstrap")

#ROC curve 2
test_prob_logtiter2 = predict(mvlogtitermodel2, newdata = CleanData, type = "response")
logtiter_roc2 = pROC::roc(CleanData$HasCryptococcus ~ test_prob_logtiter2, plot = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE)

#Calculate 95% confidence intervals, both analytically and using bootstrapping
auc_ci_logtiter2_delong <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc2, method="delong")
auc_ci_logtiter2_bootstrap <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc2, method="bootstrap")

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Sensitivity analysis: one antibody at a time
text:
Sensitivity analysis: one antibody at a time
GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM are strongly correlated, so with both in one model neither is individually significant. As a sensitivity analysis, each is modeled with sex alone (Yoon et al. 2022). These are the same specifications as models 3 and 4 above.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Given the collinearity between log_LAMIgM and log_GXMIgM, as a sensitivity analysis we explore the results of including only one of the two variables in the multivariable model, and not both:

sensitivity_table_log_lam_igm <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_LAMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData) %>%
  tbl_regression(., exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()


sensitivity_table_log_gxm_igm <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_GXMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData) %>%
  tbl_regression(., exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
text:
Optimal titer cutpoints
cutpointr() finds the GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM values, on both scales, that maximize the sum of sensitivity and specificity, with case status as the positive class. add_metric() adds the positive and negative predictive values at that cutpoint. These cutpoints are estimated on the same data used to evaluate them.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Optimized cutpoints using sum of sensitivity and specificity
cutpoint_gxm_igm <- cutpointr(CleanData, GXMIgM, HasCryptococcus,
          method = maximize_metric, metric = sum_sens_spec, na.rm = TRUE, pos_class = "TRUE")%>%
  add_metric(list(ppv, npv))

cutpoint_log_gxm_igm <- cutpointr(CleanData, log_GXMIgM, HasCryptococcus,
          method = maximize_metric, metric = sum_sens_spec, na.rm = TRUE, pos_class = "TRUE")%>%
  add_metric(list(ppv, npv))

cutpoint_lam_igm <- cutpointr(CleanData, LAMIgM, HasCryptococcus,
          method = maximize_metric, metric = sum_sens_spec, na.rm = TRUE, pos_class = "TRUE")%>%
  add_metric(list(ppv, npv))

cutpoint_log_lam_igm <- cutpointr(CleanData, log_LAMIgM, HasCryptococcus,
          method = maximize_metric, metric = sum_sens_spec, na.rm = TRUE, pos_class = "TRUE")%>%
  add_metric(list(ppv, npv))

title: Functions
text: This script defines the helper functions that export and summarize tables. None of them changes an estimate. They are new in the repository version: the original R Markdown file printed its results inline, and scripts run with source() need to save them instead.

title: Functions
text:
Save a gtsummary table
Converts any gtsummary table (Table 1, regression and merged tables) to a gt table and saves it as a self-contained HTML file. Used by Tables.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Save a gtsummary table (tbl_summary, tbl_regression, tbl_merge, ...) as a
# self-contained HTML file.
save_gtsummary_html <- function(tbl, file) {
  tbl %>%
    gtsummary::as_gt() %>%
    gt::gtsave(filename = file)
  invisible(file)
}

title: Functions
section: Save a data frame as a table
text:
Save a data frame as a table
Formats a data frame with flextable and saves it as HTML. Used for the cryptococcal antigen counts, AUC confidence intervals and optimal cutpoints.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Save a data frame as an HTML table via flextable.
save_flextable_html <- function(df, file) {
  df %>%
    flextable() %>%
    autofit() %>%
    save_as_html(path = file)
  invisible(file)
}

title: Functions
text:
Summarize an optimal cutpoint
Takes one cutpointr result from Regression, ROC and cutpoints and returns one row: the optimal cutpoint and its sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and AUC. Nothing is recomputed; the values are read from the cutpointr object.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per cutpointr result: the optimal cutpoint and its operating
# characteristics, as computed by cutpointr() and add_metric() in modeling.R,
# rounded to 3 decimal places for display.
summarise_cutpoint <- function(cp, label) {
  tibble(
    Antibody = label,
    `Optimal cutpoint` = round(cp$optimal_cutpoint, 3),
    Sensitivity = round(cp$sensitivity, 3),
    Specificity = round(cp$specificity, 3),
    PPV = round(cp$ppv, 3),
    NPV = round(cp$npv, 3),
    AUC = round(cp$AUC, 3)
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Summarize AUC confidence intervals
Takes the DeLong and bootstrap results of pROC::ci.auc() for one ROC curve and returns one row with the AUC and both 95% confidence intervals. ci.auc() returns the lower limit, the AUC and the upper limit, in that order.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per ROC curve: the AUC with its DeLong and bootstrap 95% CIs, as
# computed by ci.auc() in modeling.R. ci.auc() returns c(lower, AUC, upper).
summarise_auc_ci <- function(delong, bootstrap, label) {
  tibble(
    Model = label,
    AUC = round(delong[2], 3),
    `DeLong 95% CI` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", delong[1], delong[3]),
    `Bootstrap 95% CI` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", bootstrap[1], bootstrap[3])
  )
}

title: Clinical background
text:
Cryptococcosis is the third most common invasive fungal disease in organ transplant recipients, and carries substantial mortality (Yoon et al. 2022).
Two kinds of antibody are relevant to Cryptococcus neoformans:
Both have been associated with cryptococcosis status or risk in people with and without HIV infection (Yoon et al. 2022). In transplant recipients, Jalali et al. found pretransplant GXM-IgM lower, but posttransplant GXM-IgM and IgG higher, in patients who developed cryptococcosis (Jalali et al. 2006). This study measured both antibodies, together with total (non-specific) IgM, IgG1 and IgG2, in transplant recipients with and without a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: Clinical background
text:
Study design in brief

Setting: University of Alabama at Birmingham; recruitment 1 January 2013 to 31 December 2018.
Cases: organ transplant recipients with a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis, diagnosed by a positive cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test or body fluid culture.
Controls: organ transplant recipients with no such history.
Measurements: serum total IgM, IgG1 and IgG2 (µg/mL, Luminex); GXM- and Lam-binding IgM and IgG (titers); serum CrAg by lateral flow assay.
Approvals: the UAB Institutional Review Board approved the study, all patients gave written informed consent, and the samples were studied under an Albert Einstein College of Medicine IRB-approved protocol.

See analysis-plan.md for the full specification.

title: Clinical background
text:
References


Jalali, Ziba, Lucky Ng, Nina Singh, and Liise-anne Pirofski. 2006. “Antibody Response to Cryptococcus neoformans Capsular Polysaccharide Glucuronoxylomannan in Patients After Solid-Organ Transplantation.” Clinical and Vaccine Immunology 13 (7): 740–46. https://doi.org/10.1128/CVI.00139-06.


Torosantucci, Antonella, Carla Bromuro, Paola Chiani, et al. 2005. “A Novel Glyco-Conjugate Vaccine Against Fungal Pathogens.” Journal of Experimental Medicine 202 (5): 597–606. https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20050749.


Yoon, Hyunah, Antonio Nakouzi, Peter G Pappas, Vagish S Hemmige, and Liise-anne Pirofski. 2022. “Specific and Non-Specific Antibody Profiles in Organ Transplant Recipients with and Without Cryptococcosis.” Open Forum Infectious Diseases 9 (7): ofac211. https://doi.org/10.1093/ofid/ofac211.

title: Overview
text: Cryptococcosis is a serious invasive fungal infection after solid organ transplantation. Antibodies that bind the Cryptococcus neoformans capsular polysaccharide glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), and antibodies that bind laminarin (Lam), an algal β-glucan used as a stand-in for fungal cell-wall β-glucan (Torosantucci et al. 2005), have been associated with cryptococcosis in other populations (Yoon et al. 2022). In organ transplant recipients, one earlier study measured GXM-binding antibodies before and after transplantation (Jalali et al. 2006); laminarin-binding antibodies had not been studied. More detail is on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text: Cryptococcosis is a serious invasive fungal infection after solid organ transplantation. Antibodies that bind the Cryptococcus neoformans capsular polysaccharide glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), and antibodies that bind laminarin (Lam), an algal β-glucan used as a stand-in for fungal cell-wall β-glucan (Torosantucci et al. 2005), have been associated with cryptococcosis in other populations (Yoon et al. 2022). In organ transplant recipients, one earlier study measured GXM-binding antibodies before and after transplantation (Jalali et al. 2006); laminarin-binding antibodies had not been studied. More detail is on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text:
What this analysis does
This repository contains the analysis code for a case–control study of organ transplant recipients recruited at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB) between 2013 and 2018: 23 recipients with a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis and 21 without. Serum levels of cryptococcus-specific antibodies (GXM- and Lam-binding IgM and IgG) and of total IgM, IgG1 and IgG2 were compared between cases and controls. The results were published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Cases and controls were compared on demographics, immunosuppression and antibody levels. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression models related cryptococcosis status to antibody levels; ROC curves and optimal titer cutpoints described how well the antibodies discriminated cases from controls; and principal component analysis addressed the strong correlation between antibodies. All analyses were exploratory, with no correction for multiple comparisons. The full specification is in analysis-plan.md.

title: Overview
text:
Status
Published. This repository reorganizes the original 2022 R Markdown analysis into scripts and documents each step. The analysis code is unchanged from the published version. The study data are restricted and are not included.

This repository
The analysis was originally written as a single R Markdown file in 2022. This repository splits that file into scripts run in order by R/main.R and documents each step on this website. The analysis code is unchanged; the additions are the data path in R/setup.R, the names that results are assigned to, and the code that exports tables and figures. The study data are restricted and are not in the repository.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; open questions and known issues are tracked in Issues.

title: Figures
text:
Antibody levels by case status
The data are reshaped to one row per participant per antibody, so that all seven antibodies can be drawn in one faceted plot. Each panel shows the distribution (grey violin), the median (horizontal bar), and each participant as a point, colored by transplanted organ and shaped by sex. A Wilcoxon p-value comparing cases with controls is printed in each panel. The y-axis is log-scaled. Participants without antibody measurements are excluded.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create a long table so that all antibody titers can be placed in one or two plots
LongTiterDataNoMissingTiters<-CleanData_NoMissingTiters%>%pivot_longer(cols=TiterVariables,
                                                                       names_to = "Antibody",
                                                                       values_to="titer")

#Create pivoted plot of titer data
faceted_titer_plot <- LongTiterDataNoMissingTiters %>% ggplot()+
  geom_violin(mapping = aes(x=CaseOrControl, y=titer), color = NA, alpha=0.5,fill = "grey",
              draw_quantiles = 1)+
  stat_summary(mapping = aes(x=CaseOrControl, y=titer),fun = median, fun.min = median, fun.max = median,
               geom = "crossbar", width = 0.9, fatten=1.5)+
  geom_quasirandom(mapping = aes(x=CaseOrControl, y=titer, color=TransplantOrgan, shape=Sex), cex=2, alpha=0.7)+

title: 1. Import and clean data
text: This script reads the study workbook and derives every variable the analysis uses. It produces CleanData (all participants) and CleanData_NoMissingTiters (participants with antibody measurements), plus the variable lists used by every later script.

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Import the workbook
The study data are a single Excel workbook with one row per participant, on the sheet named Data. The file location comes from Setup, so the same code runs wherever the authorized copy is kept.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Imports data and prepares for data analysis
RawData<- read_excel(raw_data_path, sheet = raw_data_sheet)

title: 1. Import and clean data
section: Derive analysis variables and apply the exclusion
text:
Derive analysis variables and apply the exclusion
This step derives the variables used in Table 1 and the models:

Immunosuppression. The free-text regimen in Drugs is upper-cased, then three indicators are set by searching it for character strings: calcineurin inhibitor (DrugCNI: PRO, T or CYC), mycophenolate (DrugMycophenolate: M or CELL) and mTOR inhibitor (DrugMTOR: SIR or EVER). Corticosteroid use comes directly from STEROID.
Serum cryptococcal antigen. SerumCrAg holds either a titer or the word “Negative”; CryptococcalAg stores the numeric titer, with negative results set to 0.
Site of infection. CNSDisease is true when the recorded infection site (InfSite) mentions CNS.
Exclusion. One participant recruited as a control is removed because their serum cryptococcal antigen was positive. This rule comes from the original analysis code, not the published methods. It leaves the final sample of 23 cases and 21 controls reported in the paper (Yoon et al. 2022).
Outcome. HasCryptococcus is the case/control status as a logical value, the outcome for the logistic regression models.
Transplanted organ is converted to title case so that differently capitalized entries are counted together.



Click to show/hide R Code
#Data cleaning
CleanData<-RawData %>%
  #Create drug variables for CNI, mycophenolate, etc after cleaning up capitalization issues
  mutate(Drugs=toupper(Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugCNI variable is positive if drug regimen includes PRO (Prograf), T (tacrolimus), or CYC (cyclosporine)
  mutate(DrugCNI=grepl('PRO',Drugs)|grepl('T',Drugs)|grepl('CYC',Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugMycophenolate variable is positive if drug regimen includes M (mycophenolate) or CELL (Cellcept)
  mutate(DrugMycophenolate=grepl('M',Drugs)|grepl('CELL',Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugMTOR variable is positive if drug regimen includes SIR (sirolimus) or EVER (everolimus)
  mutate(DrugMTOR=grepl('SIR',Drugs)|grepl('EVER',Drugs)) %>%
  #Clean SerumCrAg variable and store numerical titer in CryptococcalAg variable
  mutate(CryptococcalAg=as.numeric(SerumCrAg)) %>%
  mutate(CryptococcalAg=ifelse(SerumCrAg %in% c("Negative", "negative"), 0, CryptococcalAg))%>%
  #Create variable for CNS disease
  mutate(CNSDisease=grepl('CNS',InfSite))%>%
  #Remove Subject 116-was control, but crypto antigen was positive
  filter(ID!=116)

#Create a binary HasCryptococcus variable for the purposes of logistic regression
CleanData<-CleanData %>% mutate(HasCryptococcus= CaseOrControl=="Case")

#We fix the capitalization issues in the TransplantOrgan variable
CleanData$TransplantOrgan<-str_to_title(CleanData$TransplantOrgan)

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Define variable groups
The categorical variables and the seven antibody measurements are named once here, so the tables and models below select them consistently. Four are cryptococcus-specific (GXM- and Lam-binding IgG and IgM, reported as titers) and three are total immunoglobulins (IgM, IgG1, IgG2, in µg/mL).


Click to show/hide R Code
#We define lists of categorical and titer variables
CategoricalVariables<-c("Sex", "TransplantOrgan", "RACE", "CaseOrControl", "STEROID", "DrugCNI",
                        "DrugMycophenolate", "DrugMTOR", "CNSDisease")
TiterVariables<-c("GXMIgG","GXMIgM","LAMIgG","LAMIgM","IgM","IgG1","IgG2" )

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Log-transform the antibody levels
Antibody levels are strongly right-skewed, so a natural-log version of each is created (log_GXMIgM and so on). The regression models use both scales; the paper’s multivariable models and ROC curves use the log scale. The list of continuous variables (age, the seven antibodies and their logs) is defined here.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Create logged versions of all titer variables
CleanData<-CleanData %>% mutate(across(TiterVariables, log, .names = "log_{col}"))

#Save the names of the logged titer variables into a list
LogTiterVariables<-paste0("log_",TiterVariables)

#Create a list of all continuous variables
ContinuousVariables<-c("AGE" ,TiterVariables ,LogTiterVariables)

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Convert categorical variables to factors


Click to show/hide R Code
#Convert appropriate variables from strings to factor variables
CleanData[,CategoricalVariables] <- lapply(CleanData[,CategoricalVariables] , as_factor)

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Participants with antibody measurements
Antibody data were missing for 2 cases (Yoon et al. 2022). Plots and analyses that need complete antibody data, such as the faceted titer plot and the principal component analysis, use this subset; missingness is identified by a missing GXM-IgG value.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create a data set where subjects with missing titer data are removed
CleanData_NoMissingTiters<-CleanData%>%
  #Filter observations with missing titer data
  filter(!is.na(GXMIgG))

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
References


Yoon, Hyunah, Antonio Nakouzi, Peter G Pappas, Vagish S Hemmige, and Liise-anne Pirofski. 2022. “Specific and Non-Specific Antibody Profiles in Organ Transplant Recipients with and Without Cryptococcosis.” Open Forum Infectious Diseases 9 (7): ofac211. https://doi.org/10.1093/ofid/ofac211.

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text: This script runs a principal component analysis (PCA) of the seven log antibody levels, then asks whether the principal components predict cryptococcosis status. The correlation plots and PCA plots are drawn in Figures, and the eigenvalue table in Tables.

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Why PCA
The antibody levels are correlated with one another, most strongly GXM-IgM with Lam-IgM (see the correlation plots in Figures), which makes their individual coefficients in a joint regression model unstable. PCA was used to account for this correlation (Yoon et al. 2022): it re-expresses the seven measurements as seven uncorrelated components. The first component, PC1, acts as a summary score of overall antibody level. It runs opposite to the antibodies, so a higher PC1 means lower antibody levels.

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Fit the PCA
PCA is run on the log antibody levels of participants with complete antibody data. scale = TRUE standardizes each antibody first, so that no single antibody dominates because of its units.


Click to show/hide R Code
#PCA analysis

#Run PCA on log of titer data
PCA<-CleanData_NoMissingTiters%>%
  select(LogTiterVariables)%>%
  prcomp(scale=TRUE)

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Component scores
Each participant’s scores on the seven components are added to the data. Figures includes a correlation plot confirming that the components are uncorrelated.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Add PCA results to CleanData_NoMissingTiters
columns<-predict(PCA)
PCAData<-cbind(CleanData_NoMissingTiters, columns)

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Do the components predict cryptococcosis?
A logistic regression of cryptococcosis status on all seven components. Because all seven are included, the model as a whole fits exactly as well as one using the seven log antibodies directly; the difference is that each component’s coefficient can be read separately. The question of interest is whether the summary score, PC1, is associated with case status.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Are the principal components predictors of cryptococcus status?
pc_regression_table <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5+PC6+PC7, family = binomial, data=PCAData) %>%
  tbl_regression(., exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
References


Yoon, Hyunah, Antonio Nakouzi, Peter G Pappas, Vagish S Hemmige, and Liise-anne Pirofski. 2022. “Specific and Non-Specific Antibody Profiles in Organ Transplant Recipients with and Without Cryptococcosis.” Open Forum Infectious Diseases 9 (7): ofac211. https://doi.org/10.1093/ofid/ofac211.

title: Setup
text: This script attaches every package the analysis uses and says where to find the study workbook.

title: Setup
text:
Packages
The package list is the one used for the published analysis:

Data import and management: readxl reads the Excel workbook; tidyverse (including stringr) handles cleaning and reshaping (Wickham et al. 2019); haven supplies as_factor(), used to turn categorical variables into factors.
Tables: gtsummary builds Table 1 and the regression tables; bstfun adds the inline forest plots to those tables; flextable formats the PCA eigenvalue table.
Figures: ggplot2, ggbeeswarm (quasirandom points) and ggpubr (Wilcoxon p-values on the plot); corrplot for correlation matrices.
Modeling: broom (attached, but not called directly by the scripts); pROC for ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals; cutpointr for optimal titer cutpoints; factoextra for PCA eigenvalues and plots.

bstfun is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub with remotes::install_github("MSKCC-Epi-Bio/bstfun").


Click to show/hide R Code
#Imports packages needed for the analysis

library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)
library(stringr)
library(readxl)
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(haven)
library(pROC)
library(broom)
library(corrplot)
library(factoextra)
library(flextable)
library(bstfun)
library(cutpointr)

text:
Constants
The study workbook is restricted and never committed. raw_data_path points to the authorized local copy, which by default sits in data-raw/, a folder excluded by .gitignore. Only the sheet named Data is used. The scripts write their outputs to tables/ and figures/.

# Output folders for exported tables and figures
